title: How to Plan Retirement When Your Income Is Irregular
description: Saving for the future on a commission or freelance budget.
content:
Standard retirement calculators assume you earn a steady salary that grows by 3% a year. For the 60 million Americans with variable income—Realtors, Sales Reps, Freelancers—this model is broken. You might earn $150,000 one year and $60,000 the next. Saving a fixed monthly amount ($500) is stressful in lean months and insufficient in flush months. To succeed, you must decouple your savings from your calendar and couple it to your revenue events.

Key Takeaways

  • The Percentage Rule: Commit to saving a fixed percentage (e.g., 20%) of every check, regardless of size. This automatically scales your savings up during 'Feast' times and down during 'Famine'.
  • The 'Floor' Contribution: Establish a tiny automated minimum ($100/mo) to keep the account active and habit alive, even in bad months.
  • The Solo 401(k) Advantage: Self-employed workers can contribute up to $69,000/year (2025). Use the 'Employer' profit-sharing bucket to dump massive lump sums at year-end to lower your tax bill.
  • Base vs. Bonus: If you have a small base salary + commission, live on the base. Save 100% of the commissions. This prevents lifestyle creep from eating your future.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Variable earners often get hit with 'Underpayment Penalties' by the IRS. A robust savings strategy includes a 'Tax Vault' where you skim 30% of every check immediately. Your retirement contribution comes after the tax skim.

The 'Feast and Famine' Flow

Stop trying to smooth your savings. Embrace the lumpiness.

Step 1: The Mandatory Skim

A $10,000 commission check arrives.
Action: Transfer $3,000 to Tax Savings. Transfer $2,000 to Retirement.
Net: You have $5,000 to live on.

Step 2: The 'Catch-Up' Quarter

In a bad quarter, you might save $0. That is okay.
In a good quarter (Q4 often), you might max out your entire $23,000 401(k) limit in one month.
Mindset: You are a 'Sniper', not a 'Machine Gunner'. You take big shots when the opportunity arises.

Step 3: The High-Yield Holding Tank

Keep 6-12 months of expenses in a HYSA (vs 3 months for salaried workers).
When the market crashes, salaried workers keep buying. You might not be able to. Your cash buffer ensures you never have to sell during a downturn to pay bills.

Tactical Setup

  1. Open a Solo 401(k): Do this at Fidelity or Schwab. It gives you the flexibility to contribute $0 or $69,000 depending on the year.
  2. Automate the Percentage: Use a bank or app that supports 'Smart Transfers'. Rule: 'When a deposit > $1,000 hits, move 20% to SEP IRA.'
  3. Prioritize Roth in Lean Years: In a year where income is low, you are in a low tax bracket. Prioritize Roth contributions. In high income years, prioritize Traditional to slash your tax bill.
  4. The 'Good Year' Rule: If you have a record year, do not upgrade your house. Fill your retirement buckets for the last 3 years (if you missed them) and the next year. Front-load your freedom.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I do a 401(k) if I'm 1099?

Yes, the Solo 401(k) is designed for you. You just can't have any full-time employees other than a spouse.

What if I can't save anything this month?

Don't stress. The Percentage Rule handles this. 20% of $0 is $0. Just stay disciplined when the big check comes.

How do I calculate my FIRE number?

Base it on your average spending over 3 years, not your income. Income varies; spending should be relatively flat.
